quizzes.title: Digital Trade Recall
quizzes.passage: Digital trade became one of the most debated areas at the recent WTO Ministerial Conference. For a long time, members had kept a standing commitment that stopped them from taxing electronic transmissions. That commitment ended at the conference because members could not agree to renew it, so the question of taxing digital goods and services is now open. Members remain divided over whether the arrangement should return in some form. The outcome also reflected a deep North-South divide among members on several issues. Some members have chosen a different route. A group of members has advanced talks on a plurilateral agreement on electronic commerce, which would bind only those members who sign it. The proposed agreement focuses on areas such as data flows, digital transactions and consumer protection. These talks have moved forward even though the moratorium itself was not renewed. Digital goods and services cover a broad range of activities. Software, music, films and digital services all fall within the moratorium's coverage. The Appellate Body, which reviews decisions made by dispute panels, has also been part of the wider debate about how the WTO resolves disputes. quizzes.title: Global findings check
quizzes.passage: Air quality around the world is often measured by the concentration of fine particulate matter, known as PM2.5, because these tiny particles can travel deep into the lungs. Health agencies set a guideline for the annual average level of these particles, and a global assessment checks how many places meet it. The assessment discussed here is prepared by a technology company that measures air quality and reports the results. Its coverage has grown over time, and the latest edition includes far more countries and cities than the earlier one did. Every reading is compared against the same guideline, so results from very different places can be placed side by side on one scale. Wider coverage matters because a place without monitors can look clean on paper while its residents breathe polluted air, and an honest comparison needs data from many locations. The findings are sobering. Only a small share of cities met the annual guideline in the latest year, and that share fell from the previous year. Most of the countries and territories assessed did not meet safe air quality standards. Only a handful of places met the guideline, and at least one city recorded very low particle levels, which shows that clean air is still possible.

quizzes.title: India's framework check
quizzes.passage: India manages air pollution through several tools that work at different stages. The first is a public information tool, a national index that converts complex pollution readings into simple categories from good to severe, so that citizens can understand the air they breathe. The second is an emergency framework. Its measures are triggered only when air quality worsens from one stage to a more dangerous one, and their purpose is to prevent further deterioration. The Supreme Court approved this emergency framework in a case concerning the environment. The third is a long-term national programme. It asks cities identified as non-attainment to reduce average particulate levels within a fixed period, and an online portal supports the tracking of its progress. The fourth is a monitoring initiative run by a government ministry, which provides city-wide and localised air quality information for major metropolitan areas and also issues weather forecasts and research. Each tool serves a different purpose, and none of them works alone. Public categories help people judge how careful to be on bad days, while emergency steps are reserved for the most severe deterioration. Long-term programmes address pollution that persists over many months and years, and monitoring tells authorities where action is needed. Together, these tools link public information, emergency response and long-term planning.

quizzes.title: Criticality and reactor choices
quizzes.passage:
A nuclear reactor produces useful power only when its chain reaction keeps going on its own. Whether this happens depends on the neutrons inside the core, because each fission releases neutrons that can trigger further fissions. Engineers track how many neutrons are produced in each round compared with the round before. If this ratio falls below the level needed, the reaction fades away. If it holds at that level, the power stays steady. If it climbs above, the output grows quickly and must be brought under control.

India's nuclear programme is designed to make the most of its resources over a long period. Early reactors use the fuel the country can readily supply, while later designs aim to create more fuel than they consume. The prototype reactor at Kalpakkam is a test of one such design, and its progress is being followed closely by scientists and policymakers.

Building a reactor that breeds fuel is demanding. Its core must be surrounded by material that captures neutrons and turns into new fuel. Its coolant must remove heat efficiently and be chosen with care, because the choice affects how the neutrons behave. These decisions shape the reactor's cost, its safety record and the amount of waste it leaves behind.

Regulation also matters. Nuclear and radiation facilities must follow national rules, and an expert body oversees their activities so that they run in a controlled way.

quizzes.title: India's energy programme
quizzes.passage:
Energy security has become a central goal for any country that depends on imported fuel. Nuclear power is one tool for this goal, because a small amount of fuel can produce a large amount of electricity. Its expansion also raises questions about waste, safety and the long-term supply of raw material. Planners have therefore looked for ways to close the fuel cycle, so that used fuel is recycled rather than simply stored. Such a plan also aims to reduce dependence on imports, which is why it attracts so much attention.

Such a plan works best when the programme is carefully staged. Each stage is meant to make better use of the country's resources than the one before it. Every stage brings its own engineering challenges, from choosing the moderator and coolant to designing the reactor core. Staging also gives engineers time to build skills and test new technology before the next step.

Nuclear facilities in the country must follow national rules and are checked by a regulator that oversees nuclear and radiation activities. The programme is described as supporting a clean, low-carbon energy transition. Progress is therefore measured not only in megawatts but also in less waste, more domestic fuel and the building of skills that place the country among the world's advanced nuclear nations.

Operators also value the ability to remain submerged for long periods and the improved survivability it offers. The submarine belongs to a family of Indian submarines that began with an earlier vessel and grew through later additions. Its construction was linked to a programme launched in the 1980s, which aimed to create an indigenous fleet of such submarines with Russian assistance. Several government bodies managed that programme, so the work drew on more than one organisation. The vessel also supports a sea-based leg of India's nuclear forces, alongside weapons delivered from land and from the air. Its role is tied to India's doctrine of not using nuclear weapons first and to the idea of a credible minimum deterrent. Readers preparing for examinations should note how these design goals, the programme history and the strategic role fit together. Taken as a whole, the vessel shows how India combines indigenous development with support from partners over several decades. Each of these points connects back to the submarine programme and the wider defence strategy.

quizzes.title: Arihant-Class Short Answer Set
quizzes.passage: Nuclear-powered submarines come in several types, and each type is built for a different role. One type carries conventional weapons, another carries guided missiles with conventional warheads, and a third carries ballistic missiles that may be nuclear armed. The third type is typically the largest and most complex of the group. Submarines of this kind are valued for stealth, which comes from low noise, along with extended submerged operations and improved survivability. India's Arihant-class submarines form part of this picture. The specifications of these submarines are classified, so any sketch of them is only an approximation, and readers should treat such drawings with caution. The class shares a design that balances power, launch tubes and displacement across its members. The programme behind these vessels aimed to create an indigenous submarine fleet with outside help. Taken together, these points show how the class fits into India's wider strategic planning. Readers studying this area often connect design features with the role each submarine plays in a country's defence. The booklet describes stealth as a benefit of these vessels, and it lists extended submerged operations and improved survivability alongside it. The class has been described in terms of its power, its launch capacity and its displacement, though some figures are not publicly confirmed. This is why sketches should be read as approximations rather than exact engineering drawings. Students should keep these categories distinct when answering questions on submarines.

quizzes.title: Artemis Programme and Accords
quizzes.passage: NASA's Artemis Programme takes its name from the Moon Goddess of Greek mythology. Its central goal is to send humans back to the Moon, including the first woman and the first person of colour to stand on its surface. The programme is carried out in stages. The first stage was an unmanned mission that launched the Orion spacecraft. A later mission carries a crew around the Moon on a flyby, after which the astronauts return to Earth. The crew will not land on the lunar surface during that flight. The crewed flight is expected to last about ten days and will end with a splashdown in the Pacific Ocean. Launches take place from the Kennedy Space Center in Florida. Plans also include a station near the Moon called the Lunar Gateway, which would serve as a docking point for astronauts and support scientific research. Several space agencies are partners in the programme, including the European Space Agency, the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency and the Canadian Space Agency. Alongside this programme, the Artemis Accords set out shared principles for peaceful exploration of space, the Moon, Mars, comets and asteroids. Many countries have joined these principles, and they were built on an older international agreement on outer space. The Artemis Accords are a framework for cooperation, and they guide how countries behave when they explore space together.

quizzes.title: Human spaceflight and Gaganyaan
quizzes.passage: Human spaceflight has a history that began in the early 1960s, when a cosmonaut from the Soviet Union became the first person to travel into space. Soon after, Alan Shepard became the first American in space as part of Project Mercury, and a woman later joined the list of people who have flown. Several other countries have since carried out their own human spaceflight efforts. India is preparing its own human spaceflight programme, called Gaganyaan, which will be India's first such programme and a new stage for the country's space work. The programme aims to send a crew into orbit for a short stay and bring them back safely. Its crew will be selected from a group of astronaut designates, and only some of them will fly on the final mission. Training for the crew takes place at a dedicated centre in an Indian city. India is also testing its systems with a humanoid robot that can monitor module parameters and raise alerts. Another tool, an application named SAKHI, will help the crew by monitoring their health, reminding them of their dietary schedules and keeping them connected with the ground. Together these tools are designed to support Indian astronauts from launch to return.

quizzes.title: Vaishali and the chess landscape
quizzes.passage: Indian Grandmaster R. Vaishali won the FIDE Women's Candidates Tournament 2026, held in Nicosia, Cyprus. With this win she became the first Indian woman to claim the Candidates title. She will now challenge the reigning champion, Ju Wenjun of China, for the Women's World Chess Championship later in 2026. Her achievement comes in a strong period for Indian chess. Viswanathan Anand, often described as India's most successful chess player, has won the FIDE World Chess Championship several times. In 2024, Gukesh Dommaraju became the World Chess Champion, making him the second Indian to win the title after Anand. Koneru Humpy, India's highest-rated female chess player, has also won major honours in the sport. The sport itself is run globally by FIDE, the International Chess Federation. FIDE acts as the global governing authority for chess, oversees all major international competitions and sets the rules and rating standards that players follow. Its motto, Gens una Sumus, means 'We are One Family'. The World Chess Championship has a long history, with its first official champion crowned in the nineteenth century. Chess players from many countries take part in its events.

quizzes.title: Digital Platforms Check
quizzes.passage:
Digital platforms faced major legal and regulatory scrutiny in April 2026. A jury in the United States found Meta Platforms and YouTube liable for designing addictive products, such as endless scrolling and algorithm-driven feeds. The ruling treated the problem as one of platform design rather than the content users posted. The court did not apply the usual shield under Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act, and the platforms were treated as products. Liability was divided between the two companies.

In India, the government has notified rules for online gaming that take effect from 1 May 2026. These rules work alongside a law that prohibits online money gaming, meaning betting and wagering, while allowing e-sports and social or casual games. Games are assessed through a determination test, and registered platforms receive a digital certificate of registration. The framework also bans advertising of money gaming and requires banks and payment gateways to block transactions linked to prohibited platforms.

The Unified Payments Interface completed ten years in 2026 and shows how digital payments are growing. It allows instant bank-to-bank transfers through mobile phones and supports both peer-to-peer and peer-to-merchant payments. Its family of products extends to several other services designed for different users.

questions.explanation: The Online Gaming Authority of India, under MeitY, is the regulator for online gaming.

The United States and Iran agreed to a temporary ceasefire after a prolonged conflict, which paused the escalation of tensions in the region. Formal peace talks were planned to follow, and they were to be led by the United States Vice President. The arrangement remained fragile. The United States kept its military forces ready for combat, and Iran warned that it could close the Strait of Hormuz again if hostilities continued. The nuclear issue also stayed unresolved, with Washington demanding the complete dismantling of key nuclear sites.

India and South Korea, meanwhile, moved their ties forward during a visit by South Korean President Lee Jae-myung. The two countries elevated their relationship to a Futuristic Partnership under a Joint Strategic Vision. Several agreements were signed, including cooperation on maritime skills and training. The partners also agreed to work together on artificial intelligence, next-generation information technology and joint research and development. Trade between the two countries is large, and South Korea has become a major investor in India. Defence cooperation includes the co-production of the K9 Vajra-T gun system, and the two sides plan to mark a shared friendship year in the future.

quizzes.passage:
India's energy and freight networks drew attention in April 2026. The Ministry of New and Renewable Energy highlighted the country's progress in renewable energy capacity, policy reforms and the wider energy transition. Solar power forms the largest part of the national energy mix, and India has built up a large stock of non-fossil capacity. The country also reported strong additions to its non-fossil capacity during the last financial year, adding to a broader push towards cleaner power. The same review also covered policy reforms, which the ministry presented as part of the country's energy transition.

Hydropower is also being revived. The Jammu and Kashmir government has moved to restore the Mohra Power Project, a historic plant on the Jhelum River in Uri, Baramulla. The move is meant to boost hydropower capacity at a time when the Indus Waters Treaty faces uncertainty. The plant is a hydroelectric power plant in the Kashmir Valley, and its revival is being pursued by the state government.

Freight infrastructure also reached a milestone. The Ministry of Railways completed the Western Dedicated Freight Corridor, which links the Jawaharlal Nehru Port Terminal in Maharashtra with Dadri in Uttar Pradesh. The Eastern Dedicated Freight Corridor runs from Ludhiana in Punjab to Sonnagar in Bihar. Both corridors are being implemented by the Dedicated Freight Corridor Corporation of India Limited.
